title: Scheduled automation and runbooks with Azure Automation
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Run your PowerShell unattended in the cloud with Azure Automation: runbooks, schedules, managed-identity authentication to Graph, and operational logging.
objectives: Explain what Azure Automation runbooks are and when to use them over local scripts
Authenticate a runbook to Graph using a managed identity instead of stored secrets
Grant a managed identity the exact Graph application permissions it needs
Import modules into the Automation account and pin versions
Schedule a runbook and pass parameters at run time
Capture output, errors, and verbose streams in job logs for operations

quiz.q: What is an Azure Automation runbook?
options: A local scheduled task on each device
A PowerShell (or Python) script that runs unattended in the cloud on Azure's compute
quiz.why: A runbook is a script hosted in an Azure Automation account that runs on managed cloud compute, on a schedule or trigger, with no local machine required.

quiz.q: How should a runbook authenticate to Microsoft Graph in production?
options: A system-assigned managed identity granted the needed Graph app permissions
A username and password stored in the script
A shared admin token pasted in a variable
quiz.why: A managed identity removes stored secrets entirely; Azure manages the credential, and you grant that identity the specific Graph application permissions it requires.

quiz.q: Why pin module versions in the Automation account rather than always using latest?
options: Pinning gives reproducible runs and prevents a new module version from silently breaking a runbook
quiz.why: Pinning the Microsoft.Graph module versions means a runbook behaves identically every run; an unexpected module update will not change behaviour or break a scheduled job overnight.

quiz.q: When a runbook uses a managed identity, which Connect-MgGraph parameter do you use?
quiz.why: Connect-MgGraph -Identity authenticates using the Automation account's managed identity, with no secret stored or prompt shown.

quiz.q: Name where you go to see what a runbook actually did, including errors and verbose output, after a scheduled run.
quiz.answer: The job history / job logs for that runbook in the Automation account, which capture the Output, Error, Warning, and Verbose streams for each run.
quiz.why: Unattended jobs have no console, so the per-job stream logs are your only window into success, failure, and diagnostics; design your runbook to write useful verbose/error output.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why are application permissions (not delegated) usually right for an unattended runbook?
quiz.answer: An unattended runbook has no signed-in user, so it needs application permissions granted to its identity with admin consent, scoped to only the operations it performs.
quiz.why: Delegated permissions act on behalf of a signed-in user; a scheduled runbook runs as itself, so it uses application permissions consented by an admin and kept least-privilege.

body_markdown:
## Why run automation in the cloud

A script that only works when *you* run it on *your* laptop is not automation — it is a chore with extra steps. **Azure Automation** hosts your PowerShell as **runbooks** that run unattended on Azure compute, on a **schedule** or trigger, with no machine to leave switched on and no one to remember to click run.

Use runbooks for anything recurring at fleet scale: nightly stale-device reports, scheduled group hygiene, off-hours remediation sweeps.

## Authenticate without secrets: managed identity

The worst thing you can do is paste a credential into a script. A **managed identity** is an Azure-managed credential attached to the Automation account; Azure rotates it and you never see it. The Graph SDK connects to it with one switch.

```powershell
# Inside the runbook — no secret, no prompt
Connect-MgGraph -Identity -NoWelcome

$context = Get-MgContext
Write-Output "Connected as $($context.AppName) in tenant $($context.TenantId)"
```

Because the runbook runs **as itself** with no signed-in user, it uses **application permissions**, not delegated ones.

## Grant the identity exactly what it needs

You grant the managed identity specific **Graph application permissions** (app roles) — and only those. This is least privilege at the identity level. The grant itself can be scripted.

```powershell
# Run once by an admin to grant the runbook's identity a Graph app role
$graphSp   = Get-MgServicePrincipal -Filter "appId eq '00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000'"
$miSp      = Get-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId $managedIdentityObjectId
$appRole   = $graphSp.AppRoles | Where-Object { $_.Value -eq 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All' }

New-MgServicePrincipalAppRoleAssignment -ServicePrincipalId $miSp.Id `
    -PrincipalId $miSp.Id -ResourceId $graphSp.Id -AppRoleId $appRole.Id
```

## Modules and version pinning

A runbook can only use modules **imported into the Automation account**. Import the Graph sub-modules you need and **pin their versions** so a surprise update never breaks a scheduled job at 2 a.m.

```powershell
# The runbook body declares what it expects; the account provides it
#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName='Microsoft.Graph.Authentication'; ModuleVersion='2.0.0' }
#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName='Microsoft.Graph.DeviceManagement'; ModuleVersion='2.0.0' }
```

Import modules via the portal, or programmatically with `New-AzAutomationModule`.

## Schedule, parameterise, and log

Attach a **schedule** (daily, weekly, or a recurring interval) and pass **parameters** at run time so one runbook serves many cases. Because there is no console, design for the **job log**: every `Write-Output`, `Write-Error`, and `Write-Verbose` is captured per job.

```powershell
param(
    [int]$StaleDays = 30,
    [string]$OutputContainerUrl
)
Connect-MgGraph -Identity -NoWelcome

$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-$StaleDays)
$stale  = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All |
    Where-Object { $_.LastSyncDateTime -lt $cutoff }

Write-Output "Found $($stale.Count) devices stale beyond $StaleDays days"
$stale | Select-Object DeviceName, LastSyncDateTime | ConvertTo-Json
```

Review the per-job streams in the Automation account's **job history** to confirm what ran and catch failures.

## Your task

Design (and where you have a sandbox, build) a runbook `Report-StaleDevices` that authenticates with `Connect-MgGraph -Identity`, accepts a `-StaleDays` parameter, lists every device stale beyond that window, and writes a JSON summary to `Write-Output`. List the **exact** Graph application permission its managed identity needs and why. Add `#Requires` lines pinning the Graph module versions, and attach a daily schedule. Describe where you would read the job log to verify the run and how you would alert on failure.

slides.narration: So far your automation runs when you run it. Now we cut the cord. Azure Automation hosts your PowerShell as runbooks that run unattended in the cloud, on a schedule, authenticating with a managed identity so there are no secrets to leak. This is how real endpoint operations run nightly reports and off-hours sweeps without anyone staying late.

slides.title: Why run automation in the cloud
bullets: Local scripts need you, your laptop, and your memory.
Runbooks run unattended on Azure compute.
Trigger on a schedule with nothing to leave on.
Ideal for recurring fleet-scale jobs.
slides.narration: A script that only works when you run it on your laptop is not really automation, it is a chore with extra steps. Azure Automation hosts your PowerShell as runbooks that run unattended on Azure's own compute, on a schedule or a trigger, with no machine to leave switched on and nobody to remember to click run. Reach for runbooks for anything recurring at fleet scale: nightly stale device reports, scheduled group hygiene, off hours remediation sweeps.

slides.title: Managed identity: no secrets
bullets: Never paste a credential into a script.
A managed identity is an Azure-managed credential.
Azure rotates it; you never see it.
Connect-MgGraph -Identity uses it directly.
slides.narration: The worst thing you can do is paste a username and password into a script. A managed identity solves this completely. It is a credential that Azure attaches to your Automation account, rotates automatically, and never reveals to you. The Graph S D K connects to it with a single switch: Connect dash M g Graph dash Identity. No secret, no prompt, nothing to leak. This one practice removes an entire category of security incidents, so make it your default for anything unattended.

slides.title: Application vs delegated permissions
bullets: A runbook has no signed-in user.
So it uses application permissions, not delegated.
An admin consents to the app roles once.
Keep them least-privilege as always.
slides.code:
# Delegated  = acts for a signed-in user
# Application = the runbook acts as itself
slides.narration: Because a runbook runs as itself, with no human signed in, it cannot use delegated permissions, which act on behalf of a signed in user. Instead it uses application permissions, also called app roles, that an administrator consents to once. The principle of least privilege still applies just as hard: grant the identity only the specific app roles the runbook actually needs, nothing more. Knowing the difference between delegated and application permissions saves a lot of confusing four oh threes.

slides.title: Grant the identity its app role
bullets: Find the Microsoft Graph service principal.
Find the managed identity's service principal.
Pick the exact app role by value.
Assign it with New-MgServicePrincipalAppRoleAssignment.
slides.narration: Granting the permission can itself be scripted. You find the Microsoft Graph service principal, that well known app id starting with triple zero three, and your managed identity's service principal. Then you pick the exact app role you want by its value, like Device Management Managed Devices dot Read dot All, and assign it with New dash M g Service Principal App Role Assignment. An admin runs this once. Now your runbook's identity can read managed devices and nothing else.

slides.title: Modules and version pinning
bullets: Runbooks only use modules imported to the account.
Import the Graph sub-modules you need.
Pin versions for reproducible runs.
#Requires declares the runbook's expectations.
slides.narration: A runbook can only use modules that have been imported into the Automation account. Import the Graph sub modules you need, and crucially, pin their versions. Why pin? Because an unattended job that always grabs latest can break silently at two in the morning when a new module version changes behaviour. Pinning gives reproducible runs. The Requires lines at the top of your runbook declare exactly which module versions it expects, documenting the contract right in the code.

slides.title: Schedule and parameterise
bullets: Attach a schedule: daily, weekly, or interval.
Pass parameters at run time.
One runbook serves many cases via params.
Same script, different inputs per schedule.
slides.narration: You attach a schedule to a runbook, daily, weekly, or a recurring interval, and you can pass parameters at run time. That means one runbook serves many cases: the same stale device report can run with thirty days for one schedule and ninety for another, just by passing a different Stale Days parameter. A well parameterised runbook is reusable infrastructure rather than a one off. Define your params at the top, just like any advanced function.

slides.title: Design for the job log
bullets: There is no console on an unattended run.
Every Output, Error, Verbose stream is captured.
Write useful output and errors deliberately.
Read job history to verify and to alert on failure.
slides.code:
Write-Output "Found $($stale.Count) stale devices"
$stale | Select-Object DeviceName, LastSyncDateTime | ConvertTo-Json
slides.narration: Because there is no console watching an unattended run, the job log is your only window into what happened. Azure captures every Write dash Output, Write dash Error, Write dash Warning, and Write dash Verbose, per job, in the job history. So design for that log: write a clear summary of what the run found and did, and let real failures surface as errors. Then review the per job streams in the Automation account to confirm success, and wire an alert on failed jobs so a broken schedule does not go unnoticed.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Runbooks run PowerShell unattended in the cloud.
Authenticate with a managed identity, no secrets.
Use application permissions, least privilege.
Pin module versions; design for the job log.
Task: design Report-StaleDevices as a scheduled runbook.

Pin your module versions for reproducibility, and design every runbook for its job log.
